incidents.cause: The loss of engine power due to cracked engine cylinder.
A total loss of engine power due to the improper use of unauthorized replacement parts in the engine and repeated operation of the engine in an over-temperature condition.

A complete loss of engine power during an agricultural application flight for reasons that could not be determined because postaccident examinations did not reveal any anomalies that would have precluded normal operation.
A loss of engine power for undetermined reasons.
Loss of engine power due to the installation of incorrect turbine blades on the compressor turbine disk during repair of the disk assembly.
The partial loss of engine power shortly after takeoff, which likely resulted from the failure of the piston connecting rod in cylinder number 3 due to hydraulic lock in that cylinder.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control on the takeoff roll, resulting in a runway excursion.
The pilot's decision to land the airplane with a crosswind that exceeded the airplane's capabilities.

The pilot’s failure to maintain adequate clearance from an object during an aerial application, which resulted in damage to the landing gear and led to the airplane ground looping during the subsequent landing.
A fractured fabricated aluminum oil line, which resulted in oil exhaustion followed by a forced landing.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during takeoff.

The pilot’s inadequate fuel planning, which resulted in a total loss of engine power due to fuel exhaustion. Contributing to the accident was the pilot’s distraction and subsequent failure to have the airplane refueled.

The pilot’s failure to maintain clearance from powerlines while flying under multiple conductors during a low-altitude aerial application flight, which resulted in propeller contact with a powerline and a subsequent loss of control.
The pilot did not maintain directional control while landing on a snow-contaminated runway.
The pilot did not reduce the airplane’s descent rate prior to the landing flare/touchdown, which resulted in a hard landing.
The pilot's failure to maintain a proper descent rate during landing, resulting in a hard landing.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control while taxiing with a gusting crosswind.
The loss of engine power during initial climb due to the pilot's improper exhaust system maintenance, which resulted in restriction of the carburetor's air intake.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during landing in gusty wind conditions that resulted in a ground loop.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control of the airplane during landing.
Insufficient available power as a result of low compression in three engine cylinders. Contributing to the accident was the pilot’s decision to takeoff with a slight quartering tailwind.
The pilot’s improper landing flare, which resulted in a bounced landing and a collapse of the left main landing gear.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during landing which resulted in a ground loop.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during an aborted takeoff.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control on takeoff.  Contributing to the accident was a lack of total experience.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll with a quartering tailwind.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during takeoff, resulting in a ground-loop, and collapse of the right main landing gear.
The pilot’s loss of directional control while landing with a gusting crosswind.
The pilot’s decision to land on a snow-covered runway.
A loss of lateral control during a hover that resulted in an impact with terrain. Based on the available evidence, the reason for the loss of lateral control could not be determined.
None.
The pilot's loss of helicopter control after entry into vortex ring state, which resulted in main rotor blade contact with the tailboom, and impact with the ground.
The pilot’s inadvertent slope landing and attempted recovery, which resulted in an incipient dynamic rollover, mast bumping, and separation of the main rotor.
The failure of both pilots to maintain directional control during landing.
The student pilot’s failure to maintain airplane control while landing in crosswind conditions and the flight instructor’s delayed remedial action.
The pilot's improper landing flare, which resulted in a bounced landing, and his subsequent failure to maintain directional control when he initiated a go-around.
